---
title: "Research"
---

My research uses geospatial artificial intelligence, satellite Earth observation, and spatial modeling to study climate impacts on Arctic settlements and infrastructure.

## Arctic infrastructure and permafrost risk

This work estimates how permafrost degradation may affect Arctic buildings and infrastructure. It combines geospatial building inventories, permafrost hazard models, and replacement-cost assumptions to assess potential mid-century damages.

Key questions:

- Where is Arctic building stock exposed to permafrost degradation?
- How do improved building inventories change estimates of climate damages?
- Which communities and infrastructure systems face the greatest potential exposure?

## GeoAI for data-scarce regions

Many Arctic regions lack comprehensive, consistent, and accessible infrastructure datasets. I use deep learning and satellite imagery to improve spatial data coverage in these areas.

Topics include:

- Building footprint extraction from high-resolution imagery.
- Model transferability across heterogeneous Arctic landscapes.
- Validation of remote sensing-derived infrastructure datasets.
- Downstream use of GeoAI products in climate risk analysis.

## Settlement change and nighttime lights

I also study settlement decline, persistence, and transformation using nighttime lights and other remote sensing time series. This research focuses especially on Russian Arctic and sub-Arctic settlements where demographic data can be incomplete, inconsistent, or difficult to access.

Topics include:

- Nighttime lights as indicators of settlement activity.
- Post-Soviet settlement decline and infrastructure persistence.
- Classification of severe population decline using remote sensing features.
- Limits of parametric models in shrinking or nonstationary geographies.

## Broader interests

- Human-environment geography
- Climate adaptation and infrastructure planning
- Remote sensing for socio-economic applications
- Spatial data science and reproducible geospatial workflows
